QF.id: Concept and Role of Mutual Fund_27

question.text:
CASE STUDY (Continued from Question 25):
Question 27: Scheme A (ELSS) is an open-ended equity linked saving scheme with a statutory 3-year lock-in, while Scheme B (Flexi Cap Fund) is open-ended. If Mrs. Sharma wants to redeem units of Scheme A before the 3-year lock-in period ends, which statement is CORRECT?

answer.text: She cannot redeem units from the AMC before the lock-in period; ELSS units have a 3-year lock-in from each investment date and cannot be redeemed during that lock-in
She can redeem units from the AMC at any time by paying a penalty of 1% of NAV as early redemption charge
She can redeem units after 1 year by forfeiting the Section 80C tax benefit already claimed
She can list the units on a stock exchange and sell them to another investor before the lock-in expires

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook classifies ELSS as an open-ended equity linked saving scheme with a statutory 3-year lock-in measured from each investment date. During the 3-year lock-in, units cannot be redeemed. Listing rules expressly exclude ELSS from the close-ended scheme listing requirement, so the lock-in is not bypassed through an exchange sale. For SIP investors, every installment carries its own 3-year lock-in from the date of that contribution. The Trap: Option B is fabricated -- there is no early redemption penalty mechanism for ELSS. Option C is wrong -- ELSS cannot be redeemed after one year, and a tax benefit once claimed cannot be reversed to enable early redemption. Option D is wrong because the listing rule for close-ended schemes specifically excludes ELSS; demat units are transferable subject to the lock-in. Note: Source pages 45 and 254 exclude ELSS from the close-ended listing rule, page 50 classifies ELSS as open-ended, page 161 supports the 3-year lock-in including per-SIP lock-in, and page 171 confirms demat units are transferable subject to lock-in.
